title: Notice pay vs garden leave - what employment contracts often get wrong
p1:
Your company asks you to leave tomorrow… but you’re still on the payroll. How does that work?

Many people assume notice pay and garden leave mean the same thing. They don’t.
p2:
Notice pay usually means an employee receives money instead of working through the notice period. Garden leave is different — the employee remains employed but is asked not to work, often to protect confidential information, clients, or business interests.

The surprising part? During garden leave, an employee may still have duties and restrictions because the employment relationship has not ended.
p3:
This difference can matter when joining a new company, handling competitors, or planning an exit. A poorly written contract can create confusion about what an employee can do after leaving a role.

The practical takeaway: always check whether your contract talks about payment in place of notice or keeping you employed during the notice period. Those two situations can have very different consequences.
conclusion: Have you ever seen an employment contract that clearly explained garden leave, or was the difference between notice pay and garden leave unclear?
